	Your technical skills are average - you handle standard smartphone features like calls, texts, email, and basic apps with ease. You understand the fundamental settings, but prefer clear, step-by-step guidance when trying something new.

	In interactions, you're naturally friendly and patient. When receiving help, you listen attentively and aren't afraid to ask questions. You make sure to confirm your understanding and provide detailed feedback on each instruction you receive.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You are unable to send MMS messages using your messaging app for the past few hours. You want to fix it and successfully send an MMS message.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently abroad in France.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

turns.thought:
I'm sorry it's still not working — let's keep digging. The data refuel definitely restored your data allowance, so if MMS is still failing there's likely a second cause. MMS is pickier than regular data — it needs a few specific settings on the phone itself.

There are a few things I'd like you to check on your phone. These are all read-only checks and won't change anything:

**1. Confirm your mobile data is actually flowing again**
Open your phone's **status bar** (top of screen) and tell me what you see. I'm looking for:
- Signal strength bars (not "No Signal")
- "Data Enabled" (not "Data Disabled")
- A network type like 5G / LTE / 4G

Alternatively, turn off Wi-Fi and try loading a webpage — if that works, data is back.

**2. Check your APN settings** — this is the #1 remaining suspect
In your phone's network settings, look up your **APN (Access Point Name)** settings and tell me:
- Whether the APN status shows "Correct" or "Incorrect"
- Whether there's an **MMSC URL** listed

The MMSC is the server that handles picture messages. If it's missing or incorrect, MMS will fail *even when regular data works perfectly* — which matches exactly what you're describing.

**3. Check Wi-Fi Calling**
Let me know whether **Wi-Fi Calling** is ON or OFF. In some cases it interferes with MMS.

**4. Check your messaging app permissions**
Tell me whether the messaging app has **Storage** and **SMS** permissions granted.

Let me know what you find on any of those and we'll fix whatever comes back wrong. If it turns out to be the APN, resetting it is a quick fix — though you'll need to reboot afterward for it to take effect. I also noticed your device was recently activated (2025-02-15) and had an eSIM transfer on 2025-01-20, so a stale setting from that transition is quite plausible.
turns.execution_output: User: Let me check my status bar first — I'll go through these one at a time so I don't mix anything up.

turns.thought:
That's a very useful finding — and it actually changes the picture. "No Signal" means your phone isn't connected to the cellular network at all, and "Data Disabled" means the mobile data switch is off. Neither of those can be fixed by adding data, so those are the real blockers right now.

The good news is your line itself is healthy on our end: it's **Active**, not suspended, and roaming is enabled. So this is a device/network-connection issue, and it's very fixable.

Let's work through this in order. Please do these on your phone:

**Step 1 — Check for Airplane Mode**
Look at the very top of your screen. Do you see an airplane icon (✈️)? If so, open Quick Settings and tap it to turn Airplane Mode **OFF**.

**Step 2 — Turn mobile data back ON**
Go to **Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections) → Mobile Network → Mobile Data** and switch it **ON**. Then confirm the status bar changes from "Data Disabled."

**Step 3 — Check your signal again**
After a few seconds, does the status bar show signal bars and a network type (5G / LTE / 4G)? If it still says "No Signal," move to Step 4.

**Step 4 — Check your SIM card**
Go to **Settings → About Phone → SIM Status** and tell me what it says (Active / Missing / Locked). If it says "Missing" or "No SIM," power the phone off, remove the SIM tray, reseat the card firmly, and power back on. If it says "Locked" (asking for a PIN or PUK), please tell me — that's something I'd need to escalate for you.

**Step 5 — Reset APN settings**
If you now have signal but MMS still fails, go to **Settings → Network & Internet → Access Point Names (APN) → Menu → Reset to Default**. Then **reboot your phone** — this step is essential for the change to take effect. Also check that an **MMSC URL** is present in the APN, since MMS won't work without it.

One tip on your data: don't worry about the 2 GB refuel — it's still on your line and will be there as soon as data starts flowing again. You were genuinely over your 15 GB limit, so you'd have needed it regardless.

Could you run through Steps 1–3 and tell me what the status bar shows afterward? If "No Signal" persists, we'll dig into the SIM and APN together, and if we still can't get you connected I'll get you over to our technical support team.

turns.thought:
Yes — absolutely, go ahead and reseat the SIM card. That's exactly the right next step, and it's the most common fix for a "Missing" SIM reading.

**How to reseat your SIM:**

1. **Power the phone completely off.**
2. Locate the SIM tray (usually on the side of the phone) and eject it using the SIM eject tool or a small paperclip.
3. Remove the SIM card and check it for any visible damage, dirt, or discoloration on the gold contacts. If the contacts look dirty, gently wipe them with a clean, dry cloth.
4. Reseat the card firmly into the tray, making sure it sits flush and properly aligned.
5. Reinsert the tray fully into the phone.
6. **Power the phone back on.**

**Then please re-check two things and tell me what you see:**
- **SIM status** — does it now say "Active" instead of "Missing"?
- **Status bar** — do you now see signal bars and a network type (5G / LTE / 4G)?

Once the SIM is detected, go ahead and **turn Mobile Data ON**, since it's currently disabled.

Two quick notes while you do that:
- Your **roaming is already enabled on your line** on our end, so there's nothing to set up there for now — we can turn on the phone-side Data Roaming setting later if you need it, but it's not relevant to getting your signal back.
- **Leave Wi-Fi off for the moment.** Having it off actually helps us test, because it forces the phone to use the cellular network — that way we'll know for sure whether the reseat worked.

Please give that a try and let me know what the SIM status shows. If it still reads "Missing" after a careful reseat, that points to a faulty SIM card rather than a seating problem, and I'll get you escalated to our technical support team to arrange a replacement — I can see there's no prior SIM replacement on this line, so a fresh card would be a clean fix.

One reassurance: the 2 GB refuel is safe on your account regardless of all this. It stays on the line until your cycle ends on 2025-02-28.

turns.thought:
Great progress — the SIM reseat worked! 🎉 "Active and working" is exactly what we wanted to see.

**Yes, please turn mobile data ON now** — that's still a blocker. Go to **Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections) → Mobile Network → Mobile Data** and switch it ON.

Then we have one more thing to fix. You mentioned you're on **2G with poor signal** — and 2G is a problem for two reasons:

- It's generally **too slow to send MMS**. Picture messages need at least a 3G connection.
- 2G often gives you that "poor" signal reading and sluggish data.

**Please also update your network mode preference:**
Go to **Settings → Network & Internet → Mobile Network → Preferred network mode** (sometimes called "Network mode") and select **5G / 4G (or "4G/5G preferred")**. If you don't see a combined option, choose **4G / LTE**.

Once you've done both, please tell me:
1. What **signal strength** are you getting now (should be better than "poor")?
2. What **network type** does the status bar show — 5G, LTE, or 4G?
3. Did **mobile data** switch to enabled?

Then try sending a picture message again.

If after that MMS still fails, the next thing we'll look at is your **APN settings** — specifically whether the **MMSC URL** is populated, since that's the single most common remaining cause of MMS failure when everything else looks fine. Resetting the APN to default (followed by a reboot) fixes that quickly.

You're very close now — the missing SIM was the root cause of the "No Service," and we've cleared that.

Yes, let's check the APN settings — that's now the most likely culprit, and it fits your symptoms perfectly: your data and signal are working fine, but MMS specifically still fails.

**Please check your APN settings:**
Go to **Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections) → Mobile Network → Access Point Names (APN)**

Then tell me two things:
1. Does the APN status show **"Correct"** or **"Incorrect"**?
2. Is there an **MMSC URL** listed? (If yes, tell me what it says; if the field is blank or missing, that's our problem.)

**Why this matters:** The MMSC (Multimedia Messaging Service Center) is the specific server that routes picture messages. It lives inside your APN settings. If it's missing or wrong, MMS will fail *even though your regular data browsing works fine* — which is exactly what you're experiencing.

**If the APN shows "Incorrect" or the MMSC URL is blank/missing, here's the fix:**
1. Tap the **menu** (three dots, usually top-right) and choose **Reset to Default** — this reloads the correct carrier settings including the MMSC URL.
2. **Reboot your phone.** This step is essential — the new settings won't apply until you restart.
3. After the reboot, confirm you have signal and data again, then try sending a picture message.

Let me know what you see in the APN screen. If resetting the APN and rebooting still doesn't get MMS working, I'll escalate you to our technical support team, since at that point we'd have exhausted the standard device-level fixes and your line, plan, and data are all in good shape on our end.

You've been patient through a good number of steps — you've already cleared the two biggest obstacles (the missing SIM and the 2G/over-limit data), so we're in the home stretch.

turns.thought:
Good question — and here's my honest read: **the URL being present and properly formed is the key thing**, and yours looks like a legitimate MMSC address (`http://mms.carrier.com/mms/wapenc` — a server endpoint for MMS routing). A missing or blank MMSC field is the classic failure we see, and that's not what you're showing.

That said, I can't independently verify from my end that this is the *exact* value your carrier provisions — so the surest way to settle it is the method you suggested:

**Yes, I'd recommend resetting the APN to default.** It's quick, safe, and definitive:
1. **Settings → Network & Internet → Mobile Network → Access Point Names**
2. Tap the **menu (⋮) → Reset to Default**
3. This reloads the carrier-published settings (including the correct MMSC URL), overwriting anything that drifted.
4. **Reboot your phone** — this is essential, the change won't take effect until you restart.
5. After reboot, confirm you have signal + data, then **try the picture message again**.

**If it still fails after that, two more things to check** — these are the remaining suspects in the MMS chain and they're quick:

- **Wi-Fi Calling:** Go to **Settings → Phone (or Connections) → Wi-Fi Calling** and tell me if it's ON. If it's ON, please turn it **OFF** — Wi-Fi Calling can conflict with MMS on some configurations.
- **Messaging app permissions:** Go to **Settings → Apps → Messages (your messaging app) → Permissions** and confirm **Storage** and **SMS** are both **Allowed**. Without Storage, the app can't attach the picture; without SMS it can't send. MMS failing in the app specifically (while data works everywhere else) is a classic permission symptom.

Let me know what happens after the APN reset and reboot — and if it's still stuck, we'll check those two. If we exhaust those and MMS is still down, I'll escalate you to technical support, because at that point your line, plan, SIM, signal, network mode, and data allowance have all been verified as healthy on our side and it'd need a deeper look.

For what it's worth, you've now cleared the three big blockers yourself — the missing SIM, the 2G network mode, and the over-limit data. That's real progress even if it doesn't feel like it yet.

turns.thought:
Yes, let's check those two now — they're the last device-level suspects before we escalate. Go ahead and check both:

**1. Wi-Fi Calling**
Go to **Settings → Phone (or Connections) → Wi-Fi Calling**.
- Is it **ON** or **OFF**?
- If it's ON, please turn it **OFF**. Wi-Fi Calling can interfere with MMS on some configurations, and since your Wi-Fi is currently off it isn't helping you anyway.

**2. Messaging app permissions**
Go to **Settings → Apps → Messages (your messaging app) → Permissions**.
Tell me which of these are **Allowed** vs **Denied**:
- **Storage** (or "Photos and videos" on newer Android)

If either is denied, please grant it. MMS failing *only* in the messaging app — while your data, signal, and browsing all work fine — is a textbook permission symptom.

After checking both, please **try sending a picture message one more time**.

**One tip while you test:** send it to a phone number on a *different* carrier if you can, and try a small photo rather than a large video. If MMS works to one recipient but not another, that shifts the problem to the receiving side rather than your line — useful information either way.

- ✅ Missing SIM → reseated, now Active
- ✅ Over-limit data (15.1/15 GB) → refueled 2 GB
- ✅ 2G network mode → set to 4G/5G
- ✅ Mobile data disabled → enabled
- ✅ APN/MMSC → reset to default + reboot
- ✅ Line status Active, no suspension, roaming enabled, contract valid through 2026-12-31

If MMS still fails after the permissions and Wi-Fi Calling checks, the remaining causes are beyond what I can resolve from here, and **I'll transfer you to our technical support team** — they can run deeper diagnostics on the MMSC provisioning and your account at the network level.

Let me know what you find on those two settings, and we'll go from there.

MMS (picture messaging) is built on top of SMS functionality, so without it the app can open, attach your photo, and look like it's working — but the send will always fail. 2. Open the messaging app and try sending your picture message again

To recap what's changed in this last round: Wi-Fi Calling is now OFF, and SMS permission is being granted. That's two more potential blockers cleared.
